moments.title: The war ends, the American century begins
moments.advantage: half of world industrial output, 80% of the gold
moments.mechanism: The only large economy not bombed produced half of global industrial output and held most of the gold, so it wrote the monetary rules and paid for Europe's recovery.
moments.outcome: Bretton Woods put the dollar at the centre; the Marshall Plan moved US$13.3 billion to 17 countries; US GDP was 1,474 billion 1990 dollars in 1945 against the USSR's 343, and 1,456 against 510 in 1950.

moments.title: The transistor at Bell Labs
moments.advantage: a solid-state switch
moments.mechanism: Three Bell Labs physicists made a working solid-state amplifier at a laboratory that employed 9,000 by the war's end and was financed by a regulated telephone monopoly.
moments.outcome: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize; Bell Labs work has since won eleven Nobel Prizes in all (a count to 2026).

moments.title: The traitorous eight
moments.advantage: the people, and silicon
moments.mechanism: Eight engineers walked out of Shockley's laboratory of 32, found a backer in Sherman Fairchild, and bet on silicon when germanium was the norm.
moments.outcome: Fairchild was founded on 18 September 1957 with $1.38 million; its first marketed transistor, the 1958 2N697, sold in a first batch of 100 to IBM at $150; by 1960 its sales exceeded $20 million.

moments.title: The planar process and the monolithic integrated circuit
moments.advantage: a manufacturable chip, patented
moments.mechanism: Hoerni's planar process let Noyce put every component on one flat silicon chip that could be mass-produced; Kilby's 1958 circuit at Texas Instruments was a hybrid, not a monolithic chip.
moments.outcome: Fairchild licensed Hoerni's planar 2N1613 across the industry, and a 1960 planar circuit with four transistors on one silicon wafer was the first silicon integrated circuit.

moments.title: The microprocessor
moments.advantage: a computer on one chip
moments.mechanism: Intel's silicon-gate process doubled circuit density, putting 2,300 transistors on one chip built for a Japanese calculator maker.
moments.outcome: The 4004 launched on 15 November 1971; Moore revised his law to a doubling every two years in 1975.

moments.title: The IBM PC and the x86 lock-in
moments.advantage: the instruction set every PC maker needed
moments.mechanism: The IBM PC used an Intel 8088; Compaq's 1986 80386 clone beat IBM to the next chip and made Intel the key supplier, after Japanese memory makers squeezed Intel out of DRAM in 1983.
moments.outcome: Intel became a microprocessor company: the 4004's field became its primary business only in the early 1980s, while IBM's 1980 gross income was $26.2 billion and Compaq's sales reached $329 million in 1986.

moments.title: The pure-play foundry
moments.advantage: manufacturing for everyone's designs
moments.mechanism: A Taiwanese government-backed joint venture, with Philips taking 27.6 percent for $58 million and the government's development fund providing 48.3 percent of the capital, built chips only for others, so any designer could start a company without a fab.
moments.outcome: TSMC held 72.5% of top-10 foundry revenue in Q2 2026 and 79% of its Q3 2026 wafer revenue came from 7nm and below.

moments.title: The GeForce 256, the first GPU
moments.advantage: a single-chip graphics processor
moments.mechanism: After nearly dying in 1996 (staff cut from 100 to 40) Nvidia put 17 million transistors on a TSMC-made chip it marketed as the first GPU.
moments.outcome: Nvidia listed in January 1999 with $0.37 billion of revenue, level with 3dfx's $360.5 million that year; in December 2000 it agreed to acquire 3dfx's intellectual assets.

moments.title: CUDA opens the GPU to programmers
moments.advantage: a programming platform on every GeForce
moments.mechanism: Created in 2004 and released in 2007, CUDA let researchers write general programs for graphics chips already sitting in their machines.
moments.outcome: CUDA was downloaded 150 thousand times in 2008, counted more than 120,000 developers in 2011, and is now 20 years old with 6 million developers.

moments.title: AlexNet on two GTX 580s
moments.advantage: deep learning only worked on GPUs
moments.mechanism: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton trained a 60-million-parameter network for five to six days on two $500 gaming cards, beating the runner-up by more than ten points.
moments.outcome: Top-5 error 15.3%; the field moved to GPUs and Nvidia's chips became research infrastructure.

moments.title: Attention Is All You Need
moments.advantage: an architecture that parallelises on GPUs
moments.mechanism: Eight Google researchers dropped recurrence, which had kept sequence models from being accelerated on GPUs; the base model trained in 12 hours and the big model in 3.5 days on eight P100 GPUs, and the advantage was published rather than kept.
moments.outcome: The big model had 213 million parameters; the paper has been cited more than 150,000 times; all eight authors later left Google.

moments.title: OpenAI scales the transformer
moments.advantage: the bet that loss falls as a power law with scale
moments.mechanism: Kaplan et al. showed loss falls as a power law in size, data and compute; OpenAI turned that into GPT-3, ten times larger than any prior dense model and 3,640 petaflop/s-days of training, on Microsoft's compute after Microsoft's $1 billion in 2019.
moments.outcome: Parameters went 117 million (2018), 1.5 billion (2019), 175 billion (2020); Microsoft licensed GPT-3 exclusively in September 2020; OpenAI was valued at $14 billion in 2021 and $29 billion in 2023.

moments.title: ChatGPT
moments.advantage: distribution: a product anyone could use
moments.mechanism: A chat interface on a scaled transformer reached 100 million monthly users in two months, with Microsoft adding $10 billion and Azure compute in January 2023.
moments.outcome: 900 million weekly users by February 2026; OpenAI valued at $29 billion in 2023, $500 billion in October 2025 and $852 billion in March 2026.

moments.title: The AI revolution reaches Nvidia
moments.advantage: every frontier lab runs on its GPUs
moments.mechanism: Demand from clouds and labs for CUDA systems took Nvidia from $1 trillion to $2 trillion in 180 days and to $5 trillion on 29 October 2025.
moments.outcome: Nvidia is valued at $4.506 trillion in November 2026; analysts project a 75% accelerator share for 2026, down from a peak near 87% in 2024.

moments.title: DeepSeek's cheaper model
moments.advantage: switching costs under test
moments.mechanism: A cheaper model trained on 2.788 million H800 GPU hours briefly broke the belief that scale needs ever more Nvidia chips.
moments.outcome: NVIDIA lost over $589 billion of market value in a day, then recovered and passed $5 trillion in October.

moments.title: The hyperscalers' capex wall
moments.advantage: customers' fear of falling behind
moments.mechanism: Five hyperscalers are forecast to spend $803 to $828 billion in 2026; Daloopa finds that over eight quarters NVIDIA's data-centre revenue equalled 39% to 47% of hyperscaler capex, 45% in the latest quarter it measured.
moments.outcome: NVIDIA's revenue was $96.2 billion in the quarter to 26 July 2026, with $279 billion of purchase commitments.

moments.title: Saratoga
moments.advantage: a victory that proved the cause viable
moments.mechanism: Burgoyne's army, 5,791 men, was surrounded by about 12,000 colonial troops and surrendered; France had already supplied up to 90% of the arms in the campaign.
moments.outcome: Louis XVI opened negotiations that produced the Franco-American alliance of February 1778.

moments.title: The French alliance
moments.advantage: a great power's navy and money
moments.mechanism: France, rebuilding its fleet for a war of revenge, signed a treaty of alliance in February 1778 and sent money, arms and troops; one account puts its direct spending on the Americans at 1.3 billion livres, another the whole war at 1,066 million.
moments.outcome: The war became a world war against Britain.

moments.title: The Chesapeake
moments.advantage: local naval superiority
moments.mechanism: De Grasse brought 24 ships of the line against Graves's 19 and held the bay; Cornwallis could not be relieved or evacuated.
moments.outcome: The British fleet withdrew and the army at Yorktown was cut off.

moments.title: Yorktown
moments.advantage: a combined army and fleet at one place
moments.mechanism: About 19,000 Franco-American troops besieged Cornwallis, with Rochambeau's 6,000 French troops and de Grasse's fleet behind them.
moments.outcome: 8,000 soldiers and 214 guns captured on 19 October 1781; peace followed on 3 September 1783.

moments.title: The debt that ended the monarchy
moments.advantage: a crown that could not tax its privileged
moments.mechanism: The American war cost 1,066 million livres by one count (1.3 billion in aid alone by another), paid by loans at high interest with no new taxes; on an income of 475 million livres the deficit was some 150 million, and by 1788 half of state revenue went on servicing the debt, while the Church held 7% of the land.
moments.outcome: The crown called the Estates-General in 1789.

moments.title: The Estates-General
moments.advantage: 98 percent of the nation, doubled in number
moments.mechanism: The Third Estate, about 98 percent of 28 million, sent 611 of 1,219 deputies, against 302 clergy and 289 nobles.
moments.outcome: The deputies became a National Assembly.

moments.title: The Bastille
moments.advantage: a crowd and a militia against a symbol
moments.mechanism: The prison held only seven inmates, but its fall was the symbol of the end of the king's command; the Assembly then abolished feudalism and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man.
moments.outcome: The Assembly took power; the Church's property was nationalised on 2 November 1789.

moments.title: The king's execution
moments.advantage: no head of state set by God
moments.mechanism: The Convention tried Louis XVI for high treason and had him guillotined at age 38; Britain, Spain and Austria were soon at war with the Republic.
moments.outcome: The First Coalition formed in 1793.

moments.title: The levée en masse
moments.advantage: a whole nation as an army
moments.mechanism: The Convention decreed a levy of about 300,000 men in February 1793, then drafted all men aged 18 to 25 in August, with 750,000 to 800,000 eventually conscripted.
moments.outcome: France fielded 1,169,000 men by 1794, against a coalition whose largest part, the Holy Roman Empire, had 800,000.

moments.title: Thermidor
moments.advantage: the Terror turning on its author
moments.mechanism: By then 16,594 official death sentences had been issued since June 1793, 1,366 of them in the last seven weeks after the Law of 22 Prairial.
moments.outcome: Robespierre and twenty-one others were sentenced on 27 July, and Robespierre was guillotined on 28 July 1794; the Terror ended.

moments.title: The coup of 18 Brumaire
moments.advantage: the army's favourite general
moments.mechanism: A bloodless coup overthrew the Directory on 9 November 1799, with 6,000 soldiers around the palace; the constitution was approved by referendum on 7 February 1800, 3,011,007 to 1,562, half a million of the votes cast by the army without valid ballots.
moments.outcome: Napoleon became First Consul.

moments.title: The Concordat
moments.advantage: the Church reconciled to the state
moments.mechanism: The Pope recognized Bonaparte's regime and the regime recognized Catholicism as the religion of the great majority of the French, while Church lands stayed seized; of the 136 old sees only 60 were kept.
moments.outcome: The hostility of devout Catholics to the Revolution ended.

moments.title: The coronation
moments.advantage: a crown taken, then blessed
moments.mechanism: The hereditary empire was confirmed by plebiscite in June 1804 (3.5 million yes, the count inflated by 300,000 to 500,000); on 2 December Napoleon crowned himself at Notre-Dame with Pope Pius VII present, omitting the formula that showed a monarch receiving his crown from the Church.
moments.outcome: Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognize the title; Austria recognized it.

moments.title: The Third Coalition
moments.advantage: Britain's money behind Austria and Russia
moments.mechanism: Britain allied with Austria and Russia in April 1805, as Napoleon's Army of England, over 100,000 men, turned east.
moments.outcome: The Grande Armée marched to Ulm and Austerlitz.

moments.title: Trafalgar
moments.advantage: seamanship and a navy that had blockaded for years
moments.mechanism: Nelson's 27 ships of the line met 33 Franco-Spanish, 18 French and 15 Spanish; 18 of the enemy were captured or destroyed and the British lost none.
moments.outcome: The invasion army had already marched into Germany in August; Trafalgar ended any real effort to invade Britain and confirmed British naval supremacy.

moments.title: Austerlitz
moments.advantage: the corps system and a lure
moments.mechanism: Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns on the field, from a Grande Armée of 350,000, against about 85,000 Allies (seventy percent of them Russian) and 318 guns, and induced them to attack; his corps, each a small army, could split and rejoin.
moments.outcome: About 36,000 Allied casualties out of 89,000 by another count (the army is 85,000 in the mechanism), 38% of their force.

moments.title: Jena and Auerstedt
moments.advantage: a modern army against a bloated command
moments.mechanism: The Prussian army awaiting the advance was about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons, but at Jena only 46,000 of them met 96,000 French, 40,000 of whom fought, out of a 180,000-strong campaign force.
moments.outcome: Prussia was crushed in a day.

moments.title: The Continental System
moments.advantage: a blockade of Britain by land
moments.mechanism: The Berlin Decree of 21 November 1806 embargoed Britain; British exports to the continent fell 25 to 55 percent against pre-1806 levels, but the loss of trade also hit France and its allies, and angry governments ignored the system.
moments.outcome: Napoleon, realising that trade ran through Spain and Russia, invaded both; the embargo ended 11 April 1814.

moments.title: Russia, 1812
moments.advantage: space, winter and a retreat
moments.mechanism: Napoleon deployed 600,000 soldiers, half of them French, against about 180,000 to 220,000 Russians in the western armies in June; the Russian army, 712,000 to 904,000 at its peak by two counts, retreated and let Moscow burn.
moments.outcome: Of 615,000, only 110,000 came back; more than 500,000 men lost.

moments.title: Leipzig, the Battle of the Nations
moments.advantage: every great power in one camp, paid by Britain
moments.mechanism: About 198,000 French (up to 225,000 by other estimates) met about 380,000 Coalition troops and 2,200 guns; British subsidies paid for a large share of the Austrian and Russian soldiers, about 450,000 at their peak in 1813.
moments.outcome: 133,000 casualties; the Coalition decisively defeated the Grande Armée; Paris fell in March 1814.

moments.title: Waterloo
moments.advantage: two armies against one
moments.mechanism: About 250,000 Frenchmen faced 850,000 allied soldiers on four fronts; at Waterloo Napoleon's 74,500 met Wellington's 74,326, then 50,000 arriving Prussians.
moments.outcome: Napoleon abdicated four days later and went to Saint Helena.

moments.title: The Congress of Vienna
moments.advantage: a balance of power restored by the victors
moments.mechanism: The five Great Powers, Austria, Britain, Russia, Prussia and France, resized each other so they could balance each other and remain at peace.
moments.outcome: The Concert of Europe, a doctrine that emphasized the balance of powers, guided European foreign policy until 1914.

story-revolutions-alliance-1778.claim: France signed a commercial agreement with the Americans, followed by a Treaty of Alliance in February 1778.

story-revolutions-allied-1815.claim: In 1815 about 250,000 Frenchmen faced about 850,000 allied soldiers on four fronts.

story-revolutions-austerlitz-allied-loss.claim: Allied casualties at Austerlitz stood at about 36,000 out of an army of 89,000, about 38% of their effective forces.

story-revolutions-austerlitz-french-forc.claim: At Austerlitz Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns, against about 85,000 Allied soldiers, seventy percent of them Russian, and 318 guns.

story-revolutions-austria-population-180.claim: The Habsburg monarchy had about 23,145,000 people around 1800.

story-revolutions-austria-subsidy-1809.claim: Britain gave Austria £250,000 in silver for the 1809 war, with a further £1 million promised.

story-revolutions-bastille-assembly-meas.claim: After the storming of the Bastille on 14 July the Assembly abolished feudalism, put the Church under state control and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man.

story-revolutions-bastille-seven.claim: On 14 July 1789 the Bastille held only seven inmates when it was stormed.

story-revolutions-berlin-decree.claim: The Continental System, a large-scale embargo of Britain, ran from the Berlin Decree of 21 November 1806 until 11 April 1814.

story-revolutions-berthier-chief-of-staf.claim: Marshal Berthier acted as Napoleon's chief of staff from 1796 until 1814.

story-revolutions-britain-budget-1814.claim: In 1814 the British budget included £10 million for the Allies and £38 million as interest on the national debt.

story-revolutions-britain-debt.claim: Britain's national debt soared to £679 million, more than double GDP, and the whole cost of the war came to £831 million.

story-revolutions-britain-subsidies-tota.claim: Total cash subsidies to Britain's allies came to £46,289,549 from 1793 to 1814.

story-revolutions-britain-subsidy-peak.claim: British subsidies paid for a large proportion of the Austrian and Russian soldiers, peaking at about 450,000 in 1813.

story-revolutions-britain-war-1803.claim: Britain declared war on France in May 1803, beginning the Napoleonic Wars, and repeatedly financed France's enemies in Continental Europe.

story-revolutions-british-army-1813.claim: At its peak in 1813 the regular British Army contained over 250,000 men.

story-revolutions-chesapeake-british-fle.claim: Graves sailed to the Chesapeake with 19 ships of the line.

story-revolutions-chesapeake-french-flee.claim: At the Chesapeake de Grasse prepared 24 ships of the line to meet the British.

story-revolutions-church-property-1789.claim: On 2 November 1789 Church property held for revenue was nationalized and used as the backing for the assignats.

story-revolutions-church-sees-1801.claim: Under the Concordat of 1801 the pope agreed to a new circumscription of the French dioceses, and of the 136 sees only 60 were retained.

story-revolutions-church-wealth-1789.claim: On the eve of the Revolution the Church held upwards of 7% of France's land and had yearly revenues of 150 million livres.

story-revolutions-civil-constitution-bis.claim: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy fixed 83 bishops, one per department, in place of 135.

story-revolutions-clergy-1789.claim: The First Estate represented 115,000 to 150,000 Catholic clergy, less than 1 per cent of the population.

story-revolutions-concert-doctrine.claim: The Congress of Vienna settlement gave birth to the Concert of Europe, a doctrine that emphasized the balance of powers and guided European foreign policy until 1914.

story-revolutions-concordat-majority.claim: The Concordat of 1801 declared that Catholicism was the religion of the great majority of the French, but not the official state religion.

story-revolutions-concordat-recognition.claim: In April 1802 Bonaparte celebrated peace and his Concordat of 1801, under which the pope recognized his regime and the regime recognized Catholicism as the majority religion.

story-revolutions-conscripts-1805-1813.claim: From 1805 to 1813 over 2.1 million Frenchmen were conscripted into the Imperial Army.

story-revolutions-consulate-palace-soldi.claim: To prevent a violent uprising by the deputies, Napoleon had the palace surrounded by 6,000 soldiers on 10 November 1799.

story-revolutions-continental-army-1775.claim: On 14 June 1775 Congress voted to establish the Continental Army, taking over 22,000 troops outside Boston and 5,000 at New York City.

story-revolutions-continental-army-peak.claim: About 250,000 Americans served as regulars or militia, but there were never more than 90,000 men under arms at any time.

story-revolutions-continental-system-eff.claim: British exports to the continent fell between 25% and 55% compared to pre-1806 levels.

story-revolutions-continental-system-inv.claim: Napoleon realised that extensive trade was going through Spain and Russia and invaded both; Russia had reopened trade with Britain in 1810.

story-revolutions-coronation-ceremony.claim: Napoleon designed a new coronation ceremony, held at Notre-Dame in the presence of Pope Pius VII, unlike the sacre of the kings of France conferred by the archbishop of Reims.

story-revolutions-coronation-date.claim: Napoleon's coronation, with the participation of Pope Pius VII, took place at Notre Dame de Paris on 2 December 1804.

story-revolutions-corps-concept.claim: Napoleon introduced all-arms corps, each a traditional army in miniature, so that the field force could split across several lines of march and rejoin or operate independently.

story-revolutions-coup-1799.claim: The bloodless coup of 18 Brumaire, on 9 November 1799, overthrew the Directory and replaced it with the French Consulate.

story-revolutions-debt-service-1788.claim: By 1788 half of French state revenue went on servicing the monarchy's debt.

story-revolutions-deficit-1789-1793.claim: Between 1789 and 1793 the annual deficit rose from 10% to 64% of gross national product.

story-revolutions-estates-deputies-1789.claim: The Estates-General of 1789 had 1,219 deputies: 302 for the clergy, 289 for the nobility and 611 for the Third Estate.

story-revolutions-estates-population-178.claim: The Third Estate, doubled in 1789, represented about 98 percent of a population of roughly 28 million.

story-revolutions-europe-populations-179.claim: By the end of the 18th century France had 28 million people, against Britain's 12 million and Russia's 35 to 40 million.

story-revolutions-fifth-coalition-1809.claim: Austria re-entered the conflict and formed the Fifth Coalition in April 1809 with Spain and Britain.

story-revolutions-first-coalition-1793.claim: In 1793 Austria, Sardinia, Naples, Prussia, Spain and Great Britain formed the First Coalition to curtail revolutionary France.

story-revolutions-first-coalition-streng.claim: The infobox of the War of the First Coalition gives the coalition's 1793 strength as 800,000+ (the Holy Roman Empire, of which Austria 500,000) and the French Republic's 1794 strength as 1,169,000.

story-revolutions-fourth-coalition-1806.claim: Prussia joined Britain and Russia in the Fourth Coalition, which resumed war in October 1806.

story-revolutions-france-debt-after-war.claim: The war raised the French government's overall debt to about 3.315 billion (livres tournois).

story-revolutions-france-direct-aid-cost.claim: France spent 1.3 billion livres to support the Americans directly, besides what it spent fighting Britain elsewhere.

story-revolutions-france-income-deficit-.claim: Before the Assembly of Notables the French crown had a total income of 475 million livres and an annual deficit of some 150 million.

story-revolutions-france-population-1780.claim: Around 1780 the population of France was estimated at around 25 million.

story-revolutions-france-population-1801.claim: The official French census of 1801 counted 29,361,000 people.

story-revolutions-france-war-cost.claim: The American war cost 1,066 million livres, financed by new loans at high interest and no new taxes.

story-revolutions-french-navy-1789.claim: In 1789 the French Navy had 71 ships of the line, with 12 more under construction.

story-revolutions-french-navy-1792-1802.claim: The French navy had 83 ships of the line in 1792 and only 46 ten years later.

story-revolutions-french-navy-1814.claim: In April 1814 the French fleet had 81 ships of the line, with 18 more under construction.

story-revolutions-french-royal-army-1789.claim: On 14 July 1789 the French Royal Army's normal strength was 172,974 men in peacetime and 210,948 in wartime.

story-revolutions-french-supplied-arms-s.claim: Estimates place French-supplied arms at up to 90% of the arms the Americans used in the Saratoga campaign.

story-revolutions-french-waterloo-army.claim: The French army at Waterloo was around 74,500, with 254 guns; Napoleon had raised about 300,000 men by June.

story-revolutions-grande-armee-1804.claim: The Grande Armée was formed in 1804 from the Army of England, a field army of over 100,000 men assembled for the invasion of the United Kingdom.

story-revolutions-grande-armee-1805-size.claim: By 1805 the Grande Armée had grown to a force of 350,000 men.

story-revolutions-jena-french-campaign.claim: Napoleon began the campaign against the Fourth Coalition by thrusting a 180,000-strong force through the Franconian Forest.

story-revolutions-jena-french-force.claim: At Jena Napoleon's force grew from 48,000 to 96,000 men, though only 40,000 took part in the battle against the Prussians.

story-revolutions-jena-prussian-army.claim: The Prussian army awaiting Napoleon's advance in 1806 was a force of about 130,000 Prussians and 20,000 Saxons.

story-revolutions-jena-prussian-engaged.claim: At Jena the Prussians had 46,000 men, and at Auerstedt 64,000.

story-revolutions-lafayette-major-genera.claim: Lafayette was made a major general at age 19 but was at first given no American troops to command.

story-revolutions-law-of-suspects.claim: On 17 September 1793 the Law of Suspects authorized the imprisonment of vaguely defined suspects.

story-revolutions-leipzig-coalition.claim: At Leipzig the Coalition armies of Austria, Prussia, Sweden and Russia decisively defeated Napoleon's Grande Armée.

story-revolutions-leipzig-coalition-forc.claim: At Leipzig the Coalition had about 380,000 troops: 145,000 to 150,000 Russians, 115,000 Austrians, 75,000 to 90,000 Prussians and 19,000 to 30,000 Swedes.

story-revolutions-leipzig-french-force.claim: At Leipzig the French had about 160,000 soldiers plus Poles, Italians and Rhine Germans, 198,000 troops in all, and other estimates run up to 225,000.

story-revolutions-leipzig-scale.claim: The Battle of Leipzig involved about 560,000 soldiers, 2,200 guns and 133,000 casualties.

story-revolutions-levee-en-masse-1793.claim: The Committee of Public Safety was formed on 6 April 1793 and the levée en masse drafted all men aged 18 to 25 into the army in August 1793.

story-revolutions-louis-executed.claim: On 21 January 1793 Louis XVI, aged 38, was beheaded by guillotine on the Place de la Révolution.

story-revolutions-marie-antoinette-execu.claim: Marie Antoinette was executed on 16 October 1793.

story-revolutions-napoleon-abdicated.claim: Napoleon abdicated four days after Waterloo, and coalition forces entered Paris on 7 July.

story-revolutions-navy-expansion.claim: After 1793 Britain doubled its frigates, added 50 per cent more ships of the line and raised its sailors from 15,000 to 133,000 in eight years.

story-revolutions-peak-austria-1809.claim: Austria's peak strength was 630,000 regulars and militia in 1809.

story-revolutions-peak-france-1813.claim: France's peak strength was 1,200,000 regulars, sailors, marines and militia in 1813.

story-revolutions-peak-prussia-1806.claim: Prussia's peak strength was 281,000 regulars and militia in 1806.

story-revolutions-peak-russia-1812.claim: Russia's peak strength was 712,000 regulars, Cossacks and militia in 1812.

story-revolutions-peak-spain-1808.claim: Spain's peak strength was 255,000 regulars and guerillas in 1808.

story-revolutions-peak-uk-1813.claim: The United Kingdom's peak strength was 380,000 regulars, sailors and marines in 1813.

story-revolutions-pitt-income-tax.claim: Pitt's income tax of 1799 raised just over £6 million against the £10 million he hoped for.

story-revolutions-plebiscite-1800.claim: The Consulate's constitution was approved by plebiscite on 7 February 1800.

story-revolutions-population-britain-fra.claim: With a population of 16 million, Britain was barely half the size of France with 30 million.

story-revolutions-prussia-population.claim: Prussia had 5,800,000 people in 1786 and 8,700,000 in 1797.

story-revolutions-recognition-1804.claim: Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognize Napoleon's imperial title; Austria recognized it in return for his recognition of Francis I as Emperor of Austria.

story-revolutions-robespierre-executed.claim: By 2 p.m. Robespierre and twenty-one Robespierrists were sentenced to death under the law of 22 Prairial, without even a cursory hearing.

story-revolutions-robespierre-guillotine.claim: Robespierre was executed on 28 July 1794, the date with which the Terror is often said to end.

story-revolutions-rochambeau-1780.claim: In 1780 Rochambeau landed at Newport with a fleet and 6,000 French troops to join Washington's Continental Army.

story-revolutions-royal-household-1788.claim: Royal household spending in 1788 was 13% of total state expenses, excluding interest on debts.

story-revolutions-russia-army-peak-1812.claim: By 1812 the Russian army reached a peak strength of 904,000, with perhaps 100,000 near Moscow.

story-revolutions-russia-initial-force.claim: Napoleon's initial force entering Russia exceeded 450,000 men, over 150,000 horses, about 25,000 wagons and nearly 1,400 guns.

story-revolutions-russia-population-1795.claim: The Russian Empire had 38 million people in 1795, after the Partitions of Poland, and 43 million in 1812.

story-revolutions-russia-survivors.claim: Of an original force of 615,000, only 110,000 survivors stumbled back; Napoleon lost more than 500,000 men in Russia.

story-revolutions-russia-western-armies-.claim: In June 1812 the disparate Russian forces led by Barclay de Tolly and Bagration totalled approximately 180,000 to 220,000 soldiers.

story-revolutions-saratoga-1777.claim: After the battles of Saratoga, Burgoyne's army totalled 5,791 men against about 12,000 colonial troops, and he surrendered it on 17 October 1777.

story-revolutions-saratoga-persuaded-fra.claim: Once news of Burgoyne's surrender reached France, Louis XVI decided to negotiate with the Americans, which resulted in a formal Franco-American alliance.

story-revolutions-second-coalition-1798.claim: A Second Coalition was formed in 1798 by Great Britain, Austria, Naples, the Ottoman Empire, the Papal States, Portugal, Russia and Sweden.

story-revolutions-sixth-coalition-losses.claim: The Grand Army lost at least 370,000 casualties in the Russian campaign, with 200,000 captured.

story-revolutions-spain-1808.claim: In November 1808 Napoleon's Armée d'Espagne of 278,670 men faced 80,000 raw, disorganized Spanish troops on the Ebro.

story-revolutions-spain-population-1800.claim: The Kingdom of Spain had 10,541,000 people around 1800.

story-revolutions-system-weakened-coalit.claim: The loss of Britain as a trading partner also hit the economies of France and its allies, and angry governments ignored the system.

story-revolutions-terror-death-sentences.claim: By the end of the Terror 16,594 official death sentences had been dispensed in France since June 1793, 2,639 of them in Paris.

story-revolutions-terror-prairial.claim: Between 10 June and 27 July 1794, after the Law of 22 Prairial, another 1,366 were executed.

story-revolutions-third-coalition-1805.claim: Britain allied with Austria, Russia and minor powers to form the Third Coalition in April 1805.

story-revolutions-trafalgar-british-flee.claim: Nelson's fleet at Trafalgar numbered 27 ships of the line and four frigates.

story-revolutions-trafalgar-fleet.claim: At Trafalgar Villeneuve fielded 33 ships of the line against Nelson.

story-revolutions-trafalgar-order-of-bat.claim: The combined fleet at Trafalgar had 18 French ships of the line and 15 Spanish ships of the line.

story-revolutions-trafalgar-result.claim: At Trafalgar 18 French and Spanish ships were captured or destroyed while the British lost none.

story-revolutions-trafalgar-supremacy.claim: Trafalgar confirmed Britain's naval supremacy in the Napoleonic Wars, and the army of invasion had already marched into Germany in August.

story-revolutions-treaty-paris-1783.claim: The Treaty of Paris was signed on 3 September 1783 by Adams, Franklin, Jay and Hartley.

story-revolutions-uk-budget-1814.claim: The British budget in 1814 reached £66 million, including £10 million for the Navy, £40 million for the Army, £10 million for the Allies and £38 million as interest on the national debt.

story-revolutions-us-population-1775.claim: The colonial population of the Thirteen Colonies had grown to 2.4 million by 1775.

story-revolutions-vergennes-secret-funds.claim: Vergennes persuaded Louis XVI to secretly fund a front company that bought munitions for the Patriots, shipped in neutral Dutch ships through Sint Eustatius.

story-revolutions-vienna-five-powers.claim: The Congress of Vienna's Concert of Europe was built on closed-doors dealing among the five Great Powers: Austria, Britain, Russia, Prussia and France.

story-revolutions-vienna-goal.claim: The goal at Vienna was not simply to restore old boundaries but to resize the main powers so they could balance each other and remain at peace.

story-revolutions-waterloo-prussians.claim: Wellington was eventually aided by the progressively arriving 50,000 Prussians who struck the French flank at Waterloo.

story-revolutions-waterloo-wellington-ar.claim: Wellington's Anglo-allied army at Waterloo had 74,326 men, of whom 27,985 were British.

story-revolutions-wellington-nearest-run.claim: According to Wellington, Waterloo was the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life.

story-revolutions-yorktown-allied-army.claim: Washington never directly commanded more than 17,000 men, and the combined Franco-American army at Yorktown was only about 19,000.

story-revolutions-yorktown-captured.claim: At Yorktown 8,000 soldiers and 214 artillery pieces were captured.

story-revolutions-yorktown-forces.claim: At Yorktown the Americans had 5,900 regular troops and 3,100 militia not engaged, the French 10,800 men and 29 warships, and the British and Germans 8,000 to 9,000.
